paper_a.title: Maximum Likelihood from Incomplete Data via the EM Algorithm

paper_b.title: A Maximization Technique Occurring in the Statistical Analysis of Probabilistic Functions of Markov Chains

metadata.description: Baum-Welch (1970) introduces the growth-transformation/E-M-style reestimation procedure for the HMM special case (probabilistic functions of Markov chains), proving monotone likelihood increase via Jensen's inequality on an auxiliary Q-function. Dempster-Laird-Rubin (1977) generalizes the same E-step/M-step iteration to arbitrary latent-variable (incomplete-data) models, names it the EM algorithm, and supplies the general convergence theory. The two papers share the same method (auxiliary Q-function, monotone-increase lemma, fixed-point/critical-point convergence) applied at different levels of generality, which is the SM (same-method) relation; DLR explicitly cites Baum et al. 1970 as the HMM special case (ExP200.7).

matches.explanation: Both state the maximum-likelihood problem with a latent/incomplete-data layer: DLR seeks argmax of L(phi)=log g(y|phi) where g is the marginal of complete-data density f over the fibre X(y); Baum-Welch seeks argmax of P_y(lambda) where lambda parametrises an HMM (A, a, f). Same problem, but DLR is general and Baum-Welch is the HMM specialisation.

DLR's incomplete-data setup (sample spaces X, Y with many-to-one map and densities f, g) is the abstract analogue of Baum-Welch's HMM setup, where the complete data is the joint state-observation sequence (x,y) and the observed data is just the y-sequence. The HMM is one concrete instance of DLR's f/g pair; DLR explicitly lists HMMs (Baum et al. 1970) under finite mixtures (ExP200.7).

Both define the auxiliary Q-function as the expectation of log of the complete-data density taken under a current parameter. DLR: Q(phi'|phi)=E[log f(x|phi')|y,phi]. Baum-Welch: Q(lambda,lambda')=int p(x,lambda) log p(x,lambda') dmu(x). Up to notational reorientation (Baum-Welch's Q(lambda,lambda') has its second argument as the optimisation variable, matching DLR's phi'), this is the same object that drives the M-step.

DLR's GEM mapping M:Omega->Omega satisfying Q(M(phi)|phi)>=Q(phi|phi) is the abstract relaxation of Baum-Welch's growth transformation T:Lambda->Lambda defined as the argmax of Q(lambda,.). Baum-Welch's T is a (full-EM) special case of GEM where the M-step is taken to be the global maximiser; DLR generalises by allowing any improvement over Q.

DLR's L = Q - H decomposition (with H(phi'|phi) = E[log k(x|y,phi')|y,phi]) is a paper-original device that does not appear in Baum-Welch. Baum-Welch instead uses a single-step Jensen-inequality bound on log P(lambda')/P(lambda) without naming an H-function or making the additive decomposition explicit.

DLR's Lemma 1 (H(phi'|phi) <= H(phi|phi) by Jensen) is stated as a self-standing lemma about the H-function. Baum-Welch uses Jensen's inequality directly inside the proof of Theorem 2.1 (PSP201.2) without isolating an H-lemma. The mathematical content overlaps but as L1 nodes they have no direct counterpart; the Baum-Welch counterpart is a proof_step (L2), so per v2 rules no L2-vs-L1 match is forced here.

These are the same fundamental monotone-increase result. DLR Theorem 1: for any GEM, L(M(phi)) >= L(phi), with equality iff Q(M(phi)|phi)=Q(phi|phi) and the conditional density is unchanged a.e. Baum-Welch Theorem 2.1: if Q(lambda,bar lambda) >= Q(lambda,lambda) then P(bar lambda) >= P(lambda), with strictness unless p(x,bar lambda)=p(x,lambda) a.e. Both are the eponymous 'EM monotonicity / Baum's inequality'; DLR extracts it cleanly from the GEM definition while Baum-Welch states it directly on the (lambda, bar lambda) pair.

Both proofs of the monotone-increase theorem use Jensen on the conditional/complete-data density. DLR splits L(M(phi)) - L(phi) into a Q-increment (>=0 by GEM) and an H-decrement (>=0 by Lemma 1). Baum-Welch uses concavity of log and Jensen on the probability measure dv_lambda = p(x,lambda) dmu(x)/P(lambda). Same Jensen-inequality core; DLR's split is the bookkeeping form, Baum-Welch's a one-shot derivation.

Composite L1-vs-L2 alignment: DLR's whole proof of Theorem 1 (PP200.2) corresponds to Baum-Welch's three-step proof (concavity of log -> Jensen -> conclude). Listed here so the reader can see the step-level correspondence on the Baum-Welch side; the parent proof match is recorded above. Confidence is medium because step granularity differs (DLR's proof bundles concavity+Jensen into one sentence).

DLR's Corollaries 1-2 say: a global (resp. strict global) maximiser of L is a fixed point of every GEM mapping. Baum-Welch's Proposition 2.1 makes the converse-direction observation: fixed points of T are critical points of P, and limit points of T-iterates are fixed points of T. Both connect MLEs to fixed points of the iteration; DLR's direction is MLE -> fixed point, Baum-Welch's is fixed point -> critical point. Together they establish the same fixed-point/MLE correspondence.

DLR Theorems 2 and 3 give convergence of GEM iterates to a stationary point of L under boundedness of L and a quadratic lower bound on Q-increments (resp. negative-definite D^20 Q). Baum-Welch's Proposition 2.1 gives the analogous limit-point statement (limit points are fixed points hence critical points of P) under continuity of T and strict monotonicity. Same global structure of convergence-via-monotonicity-plus-compactness, but DLR provides quantitative Cauchy estimates while Baum-Welch is qualitative.
DLR Theorem 4 (rate of convergence with the explicit rate matrix DM(phi*) = D^20 H [D^20 Q]^-1) has no analogue in Baum-Welch. Rate analysis is a DLR contribution beyond the 1970 Baum-Welch paper.
DLR Lemma 2 (score-function identities D^10 H(phi|phi)=0 and the Fisher-information formula) is part of the rate-of-convergence machinery (Theorem 4) and is not used in Baum-Welch.

DLR's EM Algorithm (both the exponential-family form AP200.1 and the general form AP200.2) and Baum-Welch's growth transformation AP201.1 are the same iterative procedure: starting from lambda_0, repeatedly compute the auxiliary Q-function (E-step) and re-maximise it over the parameter (M-step). Baum-Welch is the HMM specialisation with closed-form forward-backward E-step and closed-form reestimation M-step; DLR is the general latent-variable formulation. This is the central correspondence of the pair.

Composite L2 alignment of the algorithm steps under the L1 algorithm match above. The general-form E-step ASP200.4 (compute Q) corresponds to the forward-backward computation ASP201.2 that produces gamma_t(i) (the HMM-specific way of computing the Q-function). The general M-step ASP200.5 (argmax Q) corresponds to the closed-form reestimation ASP201.3. DLR's iterate-until-convergence ASP200.3 corresponds to ASP201.4. Baum-Welch additionally has an explicit Initialize step (ASP201.1) which DLR folds into the algorithm preamble. Confidence medium because of the general-vs-HMM-specific gap.
DLR's EM-for-posterior-mode variant (M-step maximises Q + log prior) is a Bayesian extension that has no counterpart in Baum-Welch's frequentist HMM treatment.

DLR's explicit definition of k(x|y,phi)=f(x|phi)/g(y|phi), the conditional density of the complete data given the observed data, is foundational to DLR's exposition but is implicit in Baum-Welch (encoded by the HMM joint factorisation).

DLR's regular-exponential-family complete-data model is a specific structural assumption used to derive AP200.1 (sufficient-statistic E-step). Baum-Welch's HMM emissions are not framed as exponential family in the abstract; the analogous structural assumption is the strict log-concavity hypothesis (TP201.2 / TP201.3) which serves a similar role in guaranteeing a clean M-step.

DLR's score-function identity DL = -E[t|phi] + E[t|y,phi] (Sundberg/Martin-Lof) and its higher-cumulant analogue are exponential-family-specific gradient/curvature formulas with no Baum-Welch counterpart.

Baum-Welch Theorem 3.1 is a structural sufficient condition (strict log-concavity in each parameter, blow-up at infinity) under which the growth transformation T is well-defined and monotone. DLR's general framework does not make an analogous coordinate-wise log-concavity assumption; the closest analogue would be the negative-definite Q-Hessian assumption of TP200.3, but the precise statement is Baum-Welch-specific.

Baum-Welch Theorem 4.1 is the location-scale generalisation (existence of unique global maximiser of Q under strict log-concavity and a non-pathology condition). It is a Baum-Welch-specific structural extension and is not present in DLR.

Baum-Welch Proposition 3.1 (global maximum of P for the shifted-Laplace family attained at a point whose components are observed y_t values) is a Baum-Welch-specific structural result with no DLR analogue.

Baum-Welch's explicit reestimation formulas (EP201.1 generic, EP201.2 forward-backward gamma_t-weighted means, EP201.3 reestimation of stochastic matrix and initial probabilities) are the HMM-specific closed-form M-step formulas. DLR's general framework does not produce these; the corresponding object on DLR side is the abstract M-step (ASP200.5) without closed form. These are the mathematical content that justifies calling Baum-Welch the HMM special case of EM.

Baum-Welch Corollary 4.1 (closed-form weighted-mean / weighted-variance reestimation for normal emissions) is a worked HMM-specific specialisation; DLR's general framework does not state Gaussian-emission formulas.

DLR's proof of Lemma 1 (Jensen-inequality bound on H) has no standalone counterpart in Baum-Welch because Baum-Welch does not isolate the H-lemma. The mathematical content (Jensen on conditional density) is reused inside Baum-Welch's Theorem 2.1 proof PP201.1.

DLR's proofs of Theorems 2 and 3 (Cauchy convergence of GEM iterates with quantitative bounds and the Taylor-series argument under negative-definite D^20 Q) are convergence-machinery proofs not present in Baum-Welch, which gives only the qualitative limit-point statement (PrP201.1).
Proofs of DLR Lemma 2 (score/Fisher-information identities) and Theorem 4 (rate matrix DM(phi*)) are part of DLR's rate-of-convergence theory, which is absent in Baum-Welch.

Baum-Welch's proof of Proposition 2.1 (fixed points of T are critical points of P, via dP/dlambda = dQ/dlambda' at the diagonal) has no standalone DLR counterpart; the analogous content is implicit in DLR's Corollaries 1-2 and is folded into the discussion around Theorem 4 rather than written as a proof of an independent proposition.
Proof of Baum-Welch Theorem 3.1 (coordinate-separable Q via sum-decomposition then apply Theorem 2.1) is Baum-Welch-specific to the additive log-concavity hypothesis and has no DLR analogue.

Proofs of Baum-Welch Proposition 3.1 (shifted-Laplace global max) and Theorem 4.1 (location-scale generalisation, boundary-behaviour + Hessian arguments) are HMM-specific structural proofs absent from DLR.
